Satellite measurements show that this year’s ozone hole over the Antarctic reached its annual maximum in mid-September and was smaller than the average of the past decade. Scientists attributed the difference to warmer-than-usual stratospheric temperatures, which limited the formation of the polar clouds that enable ozone-destroying reactions. The hole covered a maximum area of approximately 21 million square kilometers, about twice the size of Canada. Researchers emphasized that a single year does not establish a trend, but noted that the long-term record is consistent with the gradual decline of ozone-depleting chemicals following international controls. “The Montreal Protocol is working,” said one atmospheric scientist, “but recovery is slow because these compounds persist in the atmosphere for decades.” Full recovery to 1980 levels is projected for around 2066 over Antarctica, assuming continued compliance.
